subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Economics simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: the national economy, interest rates and government income and expenditure
the government's economic objectives and how they conflict
measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
fiscal policy: taxation and government spending
monetary policy, interest rates and the Bank of England

questions.lo: the national economy, interest rates and government income and expenditure
questions.q: The Bank of England raises interest rates. The most likely effect on consumers is that they:
options: Borrow and spend more, and save less
Are unaffected because rates only matter to firms
Pay less on existing variable-rate mortgages
Borrow and spend less, and save more
questions.explain: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so consumers tend to spend and borrow less and save more. This reduces demand in the economy.

questions.lo: the national economy, interest rates and government income and expenditure
questions.q: Which of the following is a direct tax?
questions.explain: A direct tax is levied on income or wealth and paid straight to the government, e.g. income tax. VAT and duties are indirect taxes charged on spending.

questions.lo: the national economy, interest rates and government income and expenditure
questions.q: A progressive tax is one where:
options: The proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises
Only firms, not individuals, pay tax
The proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises
Everyone pays the same fixed amount
questions.explain: With a progressive tax, higher earners pay a larger proportion of their income in tax (e.g. UK income tax). A regressive tax takes a larger proportion from lower earners.

questions.lo: the government's economic objectives and how they conflict
questions.q: Which of these is one of the government's four principal macroeconomic objectives?
questions.explain: The four principal objectives are full employment, price stability, economic growth and a satisfactory balance of payments. Reducing inequality and protecting the environment are further objectives.

questions.lo: the government's economic objectives and how they conflict
questions.q: A government boosts spending to cut unemployment. A likely conflict with another objective is that:
options: Inflation may rise as demand increases
questions.explain: Raising demand to reduce unemployment can push up prices, so the objective of low inflation may conflict with the objective of full employment. This trade-off is central to the spec.

questions.lo: measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
questions.q: Economic growth is usually measured by the change in:
questions.explain: Economic growth is measured by the change in real GDP, the total value of goods and services an economy produces. Real GDP adjusts for inflation.

questions.lo: measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
questions.q: In the UK, the main measure of inflation is:
questions.explain: Inflation is the sustained rise in the general price level, measured in the UK by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks the price of a typical basket of goods.

questions.lo: measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
questions.q: Rising raw-material and wage costs push firms' costs up, and they raise prices. This is best described as:
questions.explain: Cost-push inflation happens when higher costs of production force firms to raise prices. Demand-pull inflation instead comes from excess demand in the economy.

questions.lo: measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
questions.q: A worker loses their factory job because machines now do the work, and their skills no longer match available jobs. This is:
questions.explain: Structural unemployment occurs when the structure of the economy changes and workers' skills no longer match the jobs available. Frictional is short-term between jobs; cyclical is caused by a downturn.

questions.lo: measuring economic performance: growth, unemployment, inflation and the balance of payments
questions.q: A country's current account of the balance of payments is in deficit when:
options: The value of imports exceeds the value of exports
The value of exports exceeds the value of imports
questions.explain: A current account deficit means the value of what a country imports (money flowing out) is greater than the value of what it exports (money flowing in). Do not confuse this with a budget deficit.

questions.lo: fiscal policy: taxation and government spending
questions.q: Fiscal policy involves the government using:
options: Interest rates and the money supply
questions.explain: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence the level of activity in the economy. Interest rates are the tool of monetary policy.

questions.lo: fiscal policy: taxation and government spending
questions.q: During a recession, an expansionary fiscal policy would typically involve:
options: Raising taxes and cutting government spending
Cutting taxes and raising government spending
questions.explain: Expansionary fiscal policy boosts demand by cutting taxes (leaving people more to spend) and increasing government spending, helping to reduce unemployment during a recession.

questions.lo: fiscal policy: taxation and government spending
questions.q: A government runs a budget deficit when:
options: Government spending is greater than tax revenue
Interest rates equal the inflation rate
Tax revenue is greater than government spending
questions.explain: A budget deficit means the government spends more than it raises in tax over a period, so it must borrow. A budget surplus is the reverse; a balanced budget means the two are equal.

questions.lo: monetary policy, interest rates and the Bank of England
questions.q: In the UK, the body that sets the official base interest rate is:
questions.explain: The Bank of England conducts monetary policy and sets the official base rate, and works to ensure the stability of the financial system. High-street banks lend to consumers and firms.

questions.lo: monetary policy, interest rates and the Bank of England
questions.q: To reduce high inflation, monetary policy would usually:
options: Raise interest rates to reduce spending and borrowing
Lower interest rates to encourage spending
questions.explain: Raising interest rates makes borrowing dearer and saving more attractive, reducing spending and demand, which helps bring inflation down. Cutting taxes or spending changes are fiscal, not monetary, tools.

questions.lo: international trade and exchange rates
questions.q: Which is a key reason why countries trade with one another?
options: To obtain goods they cannot produce, or can only produce at higher cost, themselves
To guarantee a balance of payments deficit
questions.explain: Countries trade to obtain goods they cannot make domestically or can only make more expensively, benefiting from specialisation and wider consumer choice.

questions.lo: international trade and exchange rates
questions.q: If the pound falls in value against the euro, then for UK firms:
options: Both exports and imports become cheaper
Exports become dearer, and imports become cheaper
Exchange rates have no effect on trade
Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, and imports become dearer
questions.explain: A weaker pound means UK exports are cheaper abroad (helping exporters) while imports priced in foreign currency cost more in pounds. A useful memory aid is SPICED: Strong Pound, Imports Cheap, Exports Dear.

questions.lo: international trade and exchange rates
questions.q: According to the AQA spec, an exchange rate is determined by:
options: The size of the government budget deficit
The interaction of the demand for and supply of a currency
The Bank of England fixing it by law each day
questions.explain: The spec requires students to understand that exchange rates are set by the interaction of demand for and supply of a currency in the foreign exchange market.

questions.lo: globalisation and the global economy
questions.q: Which factor has most contributed to the growth of globalisation?
options: Advances in technology and the operations of multinational companies
questions.explain: New technology (transport, communications, the internet) and the spread of multinational companies have driven globalisation by making cross-border trade and investment easier.

questions.lo: globalisation and the global economy
questions.q: A free-trade agreement such as the EU single market mainly aims to:
options: Remove or reduce trade barriers between member countries
Increase tariffs and quotas between member countries
questions.explain: Free-trade agreements reduce or remove barriers such as tariffs and quotas between members, encouraging trade. A drawback can be increased competition for domestic producers.
